analysis.one_liner: Caps how many hogs big meatpackers can slaughter from animals they own themselves.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have capped packer-owned hog slaughter at 10 million animals a year, died in the Senate Agriculture Committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend a 1921 fair-competition law for livestock markets. It would make it illegal for any meatpacker with the capacity to slaughter more than 20 million hogs a year to slaughter more than 10 million hogs that it owns itself, with existing violators getting 18 months to comply. The point is to keep the largest packing companies from raising their own hogs instead of buying from independent farmers.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent hog farmers, who would have a larger share of the market to sell into and a fairer shot at price competition when packers can't supply themselves with their own animals. Rural communities that depend on family-scale livestock farming would also benefit if more hog sales stayed in open markets.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Independent hog farmers and rural communities

how_it_helps.text: It bars any packer with annual slaughter capacity above 20 million swine from slaughtering more than 10 million packer-owned swine in a calendar year, forcing the biggest companies to buy from independent producers instead of supplying themselves.

Packers are counted together with their subsidiaries and affiliates, and hogs owned for at least seven days before slaughter count as packer-owned, so companies could not dodge the cap by routing ownership through sister firms or short-term deals.
Packers already above the cap when the law passed would have 18 months after enactment to come into compliance, giving them time to adjust their supply arrangements.

analysis.who_pays: The largest pork-packing companies, which would have to buy more hogs on the open market from independent farmers rather than from their own vertically integrated hog operations.

drawbacks.text: Restricting packer-owned hog production could raise costs for packers, and those costs could be passed on to consumers as somewhat higher pork prices at the grocery store.
Vertical integration can offer real efficiencies in scale and quality control; forcing the largest packers to rely on open-market purchases could make some of those efficiencies harder to capture.

The bill drew no cosponsors, suggesting other senators were not persuaded that the specific 10-million-animal cap was the right line, and it received no committee consideration or hearing on the merits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a real and widely discussed problem: concentration in pork processing, where a few large companies both buy hogs and raise their own, which independent farmers have long argued depresses the prices they receive. The cost, if any, would be modestly higher packing costs and potentially slightly higher pork prices for consumers. The cap was blunt, but the underlying trade-off favors competition among farmers over integration by packers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Senator Grassley introduced the bill on September 23, 2003, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and expired at the end of the 108th Congress on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest pork-packing companies are better off, because the limit on how many hogs they could raise and slaughter themselves never became law, leaving their vertically integrated hog operations free to continue as before.

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap packer-owned hog slaughter; it was his measure alone, as it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: Thad Cochran
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration, so it never reached the Senate floor.

against.name: Large meatpacking companies
against.role: Pork processors with company-owned hog operations
against.what_they_did: Opposed limits on packer ownership of livestock during this era of the packer-ownership debate.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and the bill's only sponsor was a Republican with no cosponsors of either party, so the partisan shape of support and opposition was never tested on the record.

industries.note: Packers with capacity to slaughter more than 20 million hogs a year could no longer slaughter more than 10 million hogs they own themselves, forcing them to buy from independent producers. Independent farmers have long argued that packer ownership of hogs lets the biggest buyers avoid the open market and depress farm prices.
A cap on packer-owned slaughter would push more hog purchases into open markets, where independent farmers sell. Their income and market access depend on competitive bidding from packers.
More competitive livestock markets can benefit consumers over time, but restricting packer-owned supply could raise packing costs that get passed into retail pork prices.
